source.title: TokenFormer: Rethinking Transformer Scaling with Tokenized Model Parameters
source.authors: Haiyang Wang; Yue Fan; Muhammad Ferjad Naeem; Yong-Qin Xian; J. Lenssen; Liwei Wang; Federico Tombari; B. Schiele

record.file_problem: Whole paper text is present. Some table formatting is flattened, but the reported values can be assigned using the surrounding labels and text.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports held-out perplexity across parameter sizes for Tokenformer and downstream benchmark results at multiple sizes. It does not fit or evaluate the original scaling-law formulation; these are results for a different architecture and setup.
record.gate_note: The paper reports scaling and performance results, but does not fit power laws, test predictions from smaller runs, or find compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. The ImageNet results and architecture comparisons do not test scaling-law exponents or whether shape changes loss at a fixed parameter count. External-model comparison values are not recorded as this study's own results.
record.test_reason: This is an architecture paper. It reports perplexity and zero-shot scores for Tokenformer and Transformer baselines at a few sizes (124M–1.4B, about one order of magnitude). It fits no power law, makes no extrapolation, does no compute-optimal analysis and runs no shape sweep at fixed size. Kaplan et al. is cited only for the training procedure and for background on data scaling. Monotone improvement across 3–4 sizes of the authors' own method is method performance, not a test of any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that Tokenformer, which replaces linear projections with token-parameter attention, can be grown incrementally from 124M to 1.4B. It matches scratch-trained Transformers in perplexity (11.77 vs 11.63 at 1.4B) at much lower training cost, and is competitive on zero-shot language benchmarks and ImageNet.
record.recipe_differences: Tokenformer replaces linear projections with token-parameter attention and uses progressive parameter reuse. It does not reproduce the original scaling-law fitting or compute-optimal allocation method.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported results use distinct evaluation datasets and training setups; the paper does not analyze sensitivity of scaling-law fits to these choices.

fits_no_version.finding: Progressively growing Tokenformer by adding key-value parameter tokens reaches perplexity near scratch-trained Transformers. At 1.4B: 11.77 with 30B extra tokens vs 11.63 from scratch at 300B; 11.60 with 60B tokens.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Parameter-reuse growth reduces the compute needed to reach a given loss at larger sizes, relative to scratch training.

record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported for the relevant results. The parameter range in the held-out perplexity comparison is limited, and no power-law fit or prediction test is provided. Downstream results are benchmark scores, not a calibrated predictive relationship.
record.rows_left_out: External comparison-model results in Table 1 and Table 10 were not included because they are not reported as this study's own evaluations. ImageNet classification results were omitted because they do not measure scaling-law behavior or downstream language-task performance.

untested.parts: No power-law fit; only about one order of magnitude in parameters; no token or compute law.
No depth/width comparison at fixed parameter count.
ImageNet results at two sizes, no scaling law.
No predictive fit of downstream score on scale or loss.

record.verdict_notes: The reader mislabelled rows r1–r4: they are Transformer baselines, not Tokenformer. The relation should not be 'tests'. Its V1 limits_scope and V6 supports labels are removed, because the study does not test scaling-law claims.

versions.untested_parts: No power-law fit or exponent is reported; the parameter range is 124M–1.4B at a fixed 300B tokens on OpenWebText, not several orders of magnitude. No token- or compute-scaling law is tested.
No smaller-run fit is used to predict larger-run loss.
No compute-optimal allocation or parameter/token scaling trend is measured.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Image classification is evaluated, but no power-law scaling result is reported for images or other modalities, nor for repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
The study reports downstream benchmark scores at several sizes but does not fit a predictive relationship between pretraining loss or scale and downstream performance.
No comparison of fitting choices, exponents, or competing scaling laws is performed.

rows.subject: Tokenformer-124M
rows.operation_detail: Reports validation perplexity at 300B training tokens.
rows.note: A single size's value does not establish whether the cross-size relationship is a power law.
rows.check: Subject is wrong. In Table 7, 17.06 is the Transformer trained from scratch on 300B tokens. The Tokenformer-124M value is 16.41 at 60B tokens. These are size points, not a power-law test.

rows.subject: Tokenformer-354M
rows.operation_detail: Reports validation perplexity at 300B training tokens.
rows.note: A single size's value does not establish whether the cross-size relationship is a power law.
rows.check: Subject is wrong. 13.02 is the 354M Transformer from scratch at 300B tokens (Tables 6 and 7), not Tokenformer.

rows.subject: Tokenformer-757M
rows.operation_detail: Reports validation perplexity at 300B training tokens.
rows.note: A single size's value does not establish whether the cross-size relationship is a power law.
rows.check: Subject is wrong. 11.93 is the 757M Transformer from scratch at 300B tokens per Table 7. Table 6 gives 11.99 for the same run, so the value is inconsistent.

rows.subject: Tokenformer-1.4B
rows.operation_detail: Reports validation perplexity at 300B training tokens.
rows.note: A single size's value does not establish whether the cross-size relationship is a power law.
rows.check: Subject is wrong. 11.63 is the 1.4B Transformer from scratch. The progressively scaled Tokenformer-1.4B scores 11.77 (30B tokens) or 11.60 (60B tokens).

rows.note: One size's score alone does not show how downstream performance changes with scale.
rows.check: These are benchmark scores of the authors' own architecture (Table 1, Pile-trained). The paper fits no predictive relation between downstream score and scale or loss, so the rows do not test V6.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Tokenformer on OpenWebText at 300B training tokens, 124M–1.4B parameters
reader_labels.reason: Validation perplexity decreases across the reported sizes, but the study does not establish a power-law form or test the stated several-orders range (r1–r4).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The reported average accuracy rises with size, from 44.7 to 59.3, although no predictive fit is evaluated (r33–r36).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The reported LAMBADA perplexity falls and listed task accuracies generally rise with size; the paper does not quantify predictability (r5–r32).
